blocks.text: Your guardian hands you ₦8,000 for the term. You need a textbook, a school bag, a calculator and new sandals — and together they cost far more than ₦8,000. Deciding what to buy first is not a personal weakness. It is the whole of economics in one moment.

blocks.markdown:
**Economics** is the study of how individuals and societies allocate limited resources among unlimited competing wants.

Every economic problem starts from one stubborn fact: human wants have no end, but the land, labour, capital and time available to satisfy them are limited. Economists call this **scarcity**, and it is the reason economics exists as a subject at all.

blocks.title: Scarcity
blocks.text: A situation in which the resources available are limited relative to the wants they must satisfy. Scarcity is not the same as a temporary shortage — a commodity can be plentiful in the market and still be scarce in the economic sense, because there is never enough of it for everyone to have all they want at zero price.

items: **Unlimited** — satisfying one want simply reveals another.
**Recurrent** — you eat today and you will be hungry again tomorrow.
**Competitive** — the same ₦8,000 cannot buy both the textbook and the sandals, so wants compete for it.
**Complementary** — some wants come in pairs, such as a phone and a data bundle.
**Variable** — wants differ from person to person and change with age, income and season.

blocks.markdown:
### Free goods and economic goods

Not everything that satisfies a want is scarce. A **free good** exists in such abundance that it commands no price and needs no labour to obtain. An **economic good** is scarce, requires resources to produce, and therefore has a price.

rows: Air in the atmosphere, sunshine, rainfall
Sachet water, kerosene, textbooks, medical care
blocks.caption: Free goods carry no opportunity cost; economic goods always do

blocks.markdown:
### The scale of preference

Because resources are limited, wants must be ranked. A **scale of preference** is a list of unsatisfied wants arranged in order of priority, with the most pressing want at the top.

The scale of preference does two jobs. It forces you to admit that you cannot have everything, and it tells you exactly which want you are giving up when your money runs out.

blocks.title: Drawing up and using a scale of preference
blocks.prompt: Amina has ₦8,000. Her wants are: sandals ₦3,000, a textbook ₦5,000, a school bag ₦2,000, a calculator ₦1,500. She judges the textbook most urgent, then the bag, then the calculator, then the sandals. How many wants can she satisfy?

steps.text: Write the wants in order of priority: 1. Textbook ₦5,000  2. School bag ₦2,000  3. Calculator ₦1,500  4. Sandals ₦3,000.
Buy from the top of the list. Textbook: ₦8,000 − ₦5,000 leaves ₦3,000.
Next, the calculator costs ₦1,500 but only ₦1,000 remains, so it cannot be bought. The sandals at ₦3,000 are further out of reach.
So two wants are satisfied, and the calculator — the highest-ranked want she had to drop — is what she gave up.

blocks.answer: Amina satisfies two wants: the textbook and the school bag. The calculator is the want she sacrifices.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: Examiners regularly ask candidates to distinguish scarcity from shortage. Say clearly that scarcity is permanent and universal because wants exceed resources, while a shortage is temporary and specific — caused by hoarding, strikes, drought or price control — and can be removed.

points: Economics studies the allocation of limited resources among unlimited competing wants.
Scarcity is permanent: wants always exceed the resources available to satisfy them.
Human wants are unlimited, recurrent, competitive, complementary and variable.
Free goods such as air are abundant and priceless; economic goods are scarce and carry a price.
A scale of preference ranks wants by urgency and makes rational choice possible.
